analysis.one_liner: Bars landlords from rejecting tenants because they pay rent with vouchers, benefits, or other lawful income.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate and sent to committee in June 2019, but never received a hearing, amendment, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would add three new protected categories to the Fair Housing Act: source of income, veteran status, and military status. In practice, it targets a common practice — landlords refusing tenants whose rent comes from a housing voucher, Social Security or disability benefits, child support, or savings instead of a paycheck. Landlords would still choose tenants based on their actual ability to pay, but they could not refuse a tenant simply because part of the rent arrives from a government program or another lawful source. The bill also extends the same protections in home lending and keeps veteran-specific loan and housing programs explicitly allowed.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters who rely on housing vouchers (Section 8), Social Security, disability (SSI), Railroad Retirement, child or spousal support, trusts, or savings would have a federal right to sue if a landlord or lender rejects them because of where their money comes from. Veterans and active-duty service members gain the same shield. Because voucher holders are overwhelmingly low-income renters — often single mothers, people with disabilities, and seniors — the people most likely to use this protection are ordinary renters with the least bargaining power.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voucher holders, veterans, and benefit recipients

how_it_helps.text: Adds 'source of income,' 'veteran status,' and 'military status' as protected categories throughout the Fair Housing Act's bans on discrimination in renting, sales, and lending [S3].

Defines 'source of income' to explicitly cover Section 8 housing vouchers, federal, state, and local rental assistance, Social Security and SSI benefits, child and spousal support, payments from trusts or relatives, and savings — the lawful income sources landlords most commonly refuse [S3].
Makes it a federal crime to intimidate or threaten someone in a fair housing case based on these new categories, by extending the Civil Rights Act of 1968's intimidation provision [S3].
Preserves veteran-specific programs — including VA loan programs and VA homeless housing assistance — with an explicit carve-out so those programs can continue operating [S3].

Gives state and local fair housing agencies a 40-month window to meet federal certification requirements for enforcing the new protections, with a possible 6-month extension in exceptional cases [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Landlords and rental property owners bear the cost of compliance: they could no longer screen out tenants for using vouchers or benefits, and would face federal fair-housing liability if they did. Some smaller landlords may respond by avoiding voucher programs altogether (the voucher program is formally voluntary on their part), which could slightly shrink voucher availability in tight markets. Lenders face the same anti-discrimination rules, though the bill protects veteran-focused lending programs explicitly.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not force landlords to participate in the Section 8 voucher program, which remains voluntary; in markets where voucher payment limits fall below asking rents, landlords could still decline vouchers through that channel, limiting how much the ban changes in practice [S3].

Landlords and property-owner groups have generally opposed source-of-income mandates, arguing they add paperwork, expose owners to discrimination lawsuits over ordinary tenant screening, and can push some small owners to exit the rental market — the strongest good-faith objection to the bill (widely reported in state and local debates over similar laws).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is real but targeted: it removes a legal form of rejection that falls hardest on low-income renters, people with disabilities, and veterans, and it does so through an existing enforcement framework (the Fair Housing Act) rather than a new bureaucracy. The costs are borne mainly by landlords in the form of compliance and litigation exposure, and the practical reach depends on how many landlords simply opt out of voluntary voucher participation. This is a modest, well-targeted expansion of existing civil rights law rather than a sweeping overhaul — its main weakness is not design but the fact that it never got considered at all.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee, which took no further action on it before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021, so it died without ever coming up for a vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Tim Kaine introduced the bill on June 26, 2019, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee [S1][S5].
Two Democratic senators cosponsored the bill [S4].
No further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — appears in the bill's action history before the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Landlords who reject voucher and benefit recipients are better off, since no federal ban on that practice was enacted. The bill's backers gained nothing from the session; renters relying on vouchers or benefits gained nothing either.

for.name: Sen. Tim Kaine
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered it to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Mike Crapo (R-ID)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 26, 2019 and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and the committee that declined to act was chaired by a Republican; no votes were ever taken, so no roll-call split exists to measure the parties.

industries.note: The bill would bar them from rejecting tenants whose rent comes from vouchers, benefits, child support, or savings, and expose them to federal fair-housing liability for doing so. That protects renters but removes a screening tool landlords use, and some small owners may respond by avoiding the (already voluntary) voucher program.
Lenders would face the same anti-discrimination rules in home lending, but the bill explicitly preserves veteran-focused loan programs, so veteran lending is untouched.
